newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU-sponsored report backs oil platform removal.
newsitem.headline: EU-sponsored report backs oil platform removal.

text.p: Complete removal and land disposal of Europe's hundreds of offshore oil and gas facilities would cost $2.6 billion more than scrapping them according to minimum standards, an EU-commissioned report said.

"...Implementing the minimum requirements of International Maritime Organisation guidelines by toppling versus complete removal and disposal onshore could represent a cost differential of the order of two billion European currency units ($2.56 billion)," it said.
The report's findings were presented on Thursday to European Commission and EU member state officials, oil companies, platform designers and fisheries and environmental groups.
The two-billion-Ecu figure compares with a total cost of 18 billion Ecus to abandon offshore steel structures, itself a "relatively small sum" compared to initial construction costs.

"The study leads to the conclusion that the abandonment costs have a negligeable impact on the economics of a project and hence on the price of the oil and gas produced from these installations," the report added.

The continental shelf bordering Norway and European Union countries is dotted with 609 offshore oil and gas platforms, 430 underwater structures and 600 underwater well heads, the report said, adding that most would reach the end of their economic life within the next 30 years.

Steel platforms and subsea structures could be safely removed in their entirety, except for a very few, large, steel structures, for which an assessment of the balance between staff safety and environmental concerns would be needed.
The report added that creating artificial reefs by dumping structures on the sea bed was "not cost effective".

Environmental campaign group Greenpeace, which suffered a very public embarrassment last year when it erred in estimates of the toxic waste on Royal Dutch /Shell's disused Brent Spar platform, said the report was "a significant and positive move forward in the debate" on how to scrap old installations.
"This report shows how far the debate has moved on since the Brent Spar controversy took place," Greenpeace's Simon Reddy said in a news statement.
"It blows a hole in the oil industry's case for dumping. It shows that despite what the industry said, most large steel platforms can be removed safely and cost effectively," he said.
The Oil Industry International Exploration & Production Forum said the report was "a good basis for further discussion".
"Decommissioning remains a complex issue and it will be important not to draw simplistic conclusions from the executive summary of the report," it said in a news statement.
"The basis of the cost differential quoted in the report between sea disposal and onshore disposal for deep-water structures also needs to be clarified," it added.
North Sea consultancy Wood Mackenzie said last month that small oil exploration companies without retail operations in Britain were buying old oilfields after the Brent Spar row.
Companies without a retail presence would be less exposed to public pressure and consumer boycotts such as the one suffered by Shell last year, Woodmac said.
The report added that British taxpayers would pick up much of the decommissioning bill in the form of tax write-offs to the oil companies. ($=0.78 Ecus)
